In addition, some tables and reference entries are not cleanly formatted. These issues are noticeable but do not seriously undermine comprehension, so the section fits the adequate range.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is clear in describing broad levels of writing quality, structure, ambiguity, and APA issues. One limitation is that it combines several quite different constructs—language fluency, paragraph structure, redundancy, and APA formatting—into one scale. For grading consistency, it may help to clarify that APA problems should usually have a modest effect unless they are systematic or interfere with source tracing, especially in a course where scientific reasoning is weighted much more heavily.

intro_feedback: The introduction presents a clear and relevant research question and builds toward it with a coherent line of reasoning. It starts with societal relevance that fits the topic, defines SAD, explains why treatment access is a problem, and then develops a theoretical framework linking cognitive and behavioral perspectives to exposure-based treatment. The argument for why therapist-led and self-led VR might differ is logically developed and connected to the hypothesis. Prior research is not merely listed; the core studies are linked together and used to motivate the present design, and the additional study on self-led VR helps sharpen the gap. The main limitation keeping this below the highest range is that some claims are a bit stronger than the cited evidence fully supports, and parts of the theoretical argument are slightly stretched or speculative, especially around home-based treatment and long-term relapse prevention. In addition, the final research gap could be made even sharper by more explicitly showing why the present design solves the precise limitations of prior work. Still, the line of reasoning is clearly above adequate and convincingly argued.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric appropriately centers scientific reasoning and the coherence of the line toward the RQ and hypothesis. A useful improvement would be to distinguish more explicitly between three components that are now partially merged: societal/scientific relevance, theoretical substantiation, and literature synthesis toward the design gap. That would make grading more transparent when a paper has a clear RQ but only weak theory integration, or strong literature coverage but a weak final rationale. The rubric could also clarify how much weight should be given to responsible use of references versus depth of synthesis.
methods_feedback: The method section describes a coherent design that matches the stated research question and hypothesis: a comparison of therapist-led versus self-led VR treatment with repeated measurements over time. Participants, core inclusion and exclusion criteria, random assignment, main materials, and overall procedure are all present. The treatment section is especially useful in clarifying what differs between conditions and what was kept similar. This makes the design understandable and broadly replicable at this course level. The section is lowered somewhat because several details are underdeveloped or inconsistent. The LSAS-SR is described as a screening and outcome measure, but the explanation contains a construct error by referring to generalized anxiety disorder rather than social anxiety disorder. Important procedural details are also a bit vague, such as how randomization was implemented in practice, whether assessors remained blind throughout, and how adherence in the self-led condition was ensured. There are also realism issues in the materials description and some choices are not sufficiently justified. Overall, however, the design is coherent and mostly complete rather than conceptually flawed.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric captures coherence and completeness well, but the distinctions between developing, adequate, and good are somewhat broad. It would help to specify a few anchor elements expected at this course level, such as inclusion/exclusion criteria, allocation to conditions, operationalization of variables, and enough procedural detail for rough replication. That would make judgments more consistent and reduce assessor variation when a method is coherent overall but missing one or two key details.
results_feedback: The results section is largely in line with the expected sample structure: it reports sample use, outlier checks, descriptive information, the main mixed ANOVA, assumption checks, interaction interpretation, and post hoc comparisons. The analyses are appropriate for the stated design and clearly linked to the research question. The reporting is understandable and the narrative of the findings is easy to follow. This supports a grade in the good range. The main reasons it does not score higher are omissions in presentation and some reporting limitations. Table 1 and Table 2 are referred to, but in the text body the formatting is incomplete and not fully integrated in a polished way. The results rely heavily on significance testing without giving richer statistical detail such as effect sizes. Some assumption reporting is brief, and the section does not fully reach the level of completeness and polish of the sample results. Still, the core analysis and interpretation are correct and coherent for this course level.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is sensible, especially because it emphasizes appropriateness relative to the stated design. It could be improved by adding clearer anchors tied to the course sample, such as descriptive tables, assumption checks, reporting of the main test, and interpretation of interaction/post hoc results where relevant. At present, the difference between adequate and good may depend too much on assessor intuition about completeness. More explicit expectations for student-level statistical reporting would increase reliability.
discussion_feedback: The discussion gives a clear answer to the research question, states whether the hypothesis was supported, and interprets the findings at the construct level rather than simply repeating the results. It compares the findings to previous literature and links them back to the theoretical perspectives introduced earlier. The discussion also handles the unexpected part of the findings—the maintenance of self-led gains over time—by offering a plausible explanation grounded in differences in exposure breadth and transfer/generalization. The section includes meaningful limitations and concrete future research suggestions, especially regarding the lack of a waiting-list control and the inability to monitor engagement in self-led VR. Broader implications are also addressed in a balanced way. The main limitation is that some interpretations go further than the design warrants, especially when suggesting spontaneous recovery or regression to the mean without direct evidence, and some theoretical claims remain somewhat speculative. Even so, the reasoning is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued overall.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric correctly prioritizes the coherence of the main conclusion and the relevance of critical reflection. A useful refinement would be to make explicit that strong discussions should not only restate whether the hypothesis was supported, but also interpret unexpected findings, connect back to the introduction's theory, and provide study-specific limitations and future directions. These features are implied but not fully operationalized in the current wording, which may lead to uneven grading across assessors.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is clearly readable and generally uses appropriate scientific language. The structure is easy to follow across sections, paragraph focus is mostly maintained, and transitions are generally functional. Grammar and spelling errors are limited and do not impede understanding. However, the writing is not near-faultless. There are several APA and formatting issues in both the text and reference list, including inconsistent citation formatting, inconsistent year/details for some sources, incomplete journal formatting, and visible table placement/layout problems. There are also some awkward phrasings and occasional redundancy. Because the text remains clear and mostly well structured despite these issues, the paper fits best in the adequate-to-good range, with the APA/layout issues keeping it from a higher score.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed, but some descriptors remain subjective, especially terms like 'near faultless' and 'graceful style.' For better interrater consistency, it may help to separate clarity/structure from APA/formatting more explicitly, or to provide concrete anchors for how much APA error is compatible with each level. Since style has a smaller weight in the overall grading philosophy, the rubric might also note more clearly that language issues should only substantially lower the score when they interfere with comprehension or professional presentation.

intro_feedback: The Introduction is strong on scientific reasoning for this course level. It presents a clear societal relevance, defines SAD, explains why treatment access is a problem, and builds a coherent theoretical line from CBT and exposure mechanisms toward VR treatment. The transition from therapist-led VR to self-led VR is logical, and the final research question and hypothesis are clearly stated and well aligned with the preceding argumentation. The required core studies are integrated meaningfully rather than only summarized, and the student also uses an additional study to motivate the specific comparison. What keeps this below the highest range is that some claims are argued somewhat too strongly relative to the evidence provided, especially around long-term maintenance and the supposed role of therapist personalization. In addition, some literature choices are not optimally aligned with the exact design, and parts of the theoretical framework remain more descriptive than fully synthesized into a sharper prediction. Still, the line of reasoning is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued overall.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is useful because it centers grading on the line of reasoning culminating in the research question, relevance, and hypothesis, which fits the course goals well. A possible improvement would be to make literature synthesis more explicit as a criterion, because students can appear coherent while still writing a study-by-study summary. It may also help to specify how much weight should be given to theoretical integration versus societal relevance, since both are currently bundled under one broad criterion. Finally, the distinction between 'adequate' and 'good' could be operationalized more concretely with examples of what counts as merely coherent versus convincingly argued.
methods_feedback: The Methods section is coherent and mostly related to the stated research question and hypothesis, but it has several weaknesses that prevent a higher score. The participant section includes recruitment, sample characteristics, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and random allocation, which fits the rubric well. The procedure is also broadly chronological and understandable. However, there are important completeness and precision issues. The LSAS-SR is described inaccurately as a screening tool for generalized anxiety disorder rather than social anxiety disorder, which is a meaningful conceptual error. The use of screening LSAS-SR scores as pre-treatment scores raises design concerns, because screening and baseline measurement are not necessarily equivalent. The intervention description is reasonably detailed, but some aspects of standardization and comparability between conditions remain vague, especially because location and guidance both differ between conditions, introducing confounds that are not acknowledged in the method. Ethical approval is mentioned only vaguely, and some procedural details that matter for replication are underdeveloped. Overall, the study design is understandable and mostly complete, but not fully correct or fully controlled.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately emphasizes coherence with the research question and the completeness/correctness of participants, materials, and procedure. To improve grading consistency, the rubric could define more clearly what counts as 'complete' at this student level, for example by listing essential elements such as allocation, inclusion/exclusion criteria, operationalization of conditions, and timing of measurements. It would also help if the rubric distinguished more explicitly between minor omissions and conceptual design flaws, because both can currently fall under similar wording. Adding guidance about confounds and internal validity would strengthen alignment with scientific reasoning goals.
results_feedback: The Results section is mostly correct, coherent, and relevant to the stated design. It includes the sample size, outlier check, descriptive information, the main factorial mixed ANOVA, assumption checks, interaction interpretation, and post hoc comparisons. This follows the expected course template reasonably well and gives a clear answer to the hypothesis. The reporting is understandable, and the main pattern in the data is easy to follow. However, the section is less complete and polished than a stronger 'good' result section. The tables and figure are referred to appropriately, but the actual presentation is incomplete in the body of the paper format provided here, which weakens clarity. Some reporting is also somewhat sparse: effect sizes are absent, the assumption checks are brief, and the ANOVA description could be more precise. There is also a tension between the statistical significance of the self-led maintenance effect and the later interpretive caution in the Discussion, which makes the practical meaning of the results feel less fully integrated. Still, at this student level, the core statistical reasoning and reporting are adequate to good.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric captures the core issues well: correctness, completeness, coherence, and relevance to the stated design. It is especially helpful that the calibration materials supplement the rubric with a sample results section, because the rubric alone is still somewhat broad. A useful improvement would be to specify expected reporting elements for this course, such as descriptives, assumption checks, test statistics, post hoc tests, and visual or tabular presentation. That would make the distinction between 'adequate' and 'good' less subjective. It may also help to clarify whether missing effect sizes or incomplete tables should meaningfully affect the score at this level.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion shows solid scientific reasoning and a generally coherent interpretation of the findings. It opens with a clear answer to the research question, distinguishes between supported and partially unsupported parts of the hypothesis, and connects the findings back to prior literature and theory. The student does more than restate results: they interpret the stronger therapist-led effect via mechanisms such as personalization, safety behavior reduction, and integration of cognitive and exposure components. The discussion of the unexpected maintenance of self-led gains is a clear strength, because it attempts to explain divergence from prior research using design differences. The section also includes relevant limitations and concrete future directions, especially regarding the lack of a waiting-list control and the inability to measure engagement in the self-led condition. What keeps the score below the top range is that some interpretations overreach the actual design, particularly when attributing causal mechanisms that were not directly measured. One limitation argument also comes close to challenging the validity of the observed self-led effect in a way that could have been more tightly reasoned from the data. Overall, though, the main conclusion is correct, coherent, and critically reflected upon.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric is strong in focusing on the reasoning toward the main conclusion and the relevance of critical reflection. However, it remains somewhat broad about what qualifies as a convincing critical reflection. The rubric could be improved by explicitly mentioning expected components such as linking findings to prior research, discussing theory, addressing unexpected findings, identifying study-specific limitations, and proposing concrete future research. That would align it even more closely with the writing guide and help distinguish between a discussion that is merely correct and one that is genuinely strong.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally readable, well structured, and mostly uses appropriate scientific language. Paragraphs usually have a clear focus, and the overall organization of the paper is easy to follow. The writing is stronger than average for this level in terms of flow and coherence. However, there are several language and APA issues that lower the score. Some phrasing is awkward or imprecise, and there are noticeable inconsistencies in reference formatting, punctuation, capitalization, publication years, and citation style. A few source details appear inaccurate or inconsistently reported. There are also minor wording issues in the methods and discussion that reduce precision. None of these problems seriously impede understanding, but they are too frequent for a higher language/style score.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is comprehensive and helpful because it captures clarity, structure, grammar, APA, vagueness, and redundancy. Still, some categories overlap, which can make grading feel diffuse. It may help to separate readability/structure from APA/technical correctness more explicitly, especially since APA errors are less central to course learning goals than scientific reasoning. In addition, the jump from 'adequate' to 'good' relies on somewhat subjective terms such as 'near faultless'; more concrete anchors or examples would improve inter-rater consistency.

intro_feedback:
The introduction presents a clear and mostly coherent line of reasoning toward the research question and hypothesis. Societal relevance is stated early and is aligned with the proposed design: if people with SAD avoid treatment, a more accessible at-home VR format is a relevant problem to study. The paper also includes a theoretical basis, covering cognitive and behavioral accounts of SAD and linking exposure to extinction and relapse prevention. This gives the hypothesis some real theoretical grounding rather than making it purely empirical. The research question and hypothesis are clearly stated at the end and follow logically from the preceding argument.

The strongest aspect is that the prior research section is not just a list of studies. The student does make some effort to use the core articles as building blocks: Kampmann is used to argue that stand-alone VR may be weaker than in vivo, Anderson is used to introduce the possible role of cognitive therapy, and Bouchard is used to support generalization to broader social fears. The extra study by Lindner is then used to motivate the therapist-led versus self-led comparison. That overall argumentative flow supports a Good-level grade.

What prevents a higher grade is that several links are still somewhat weak or overstated. Some claims are more assertive than the evidence provided warrants, for example the leap from smartphone-enabled VR being accessible to the proposed home-based self-led intervention, and the assumption that therapist input necessarily produces better long-term outcomes. Theoretical integration is present, but not always tightly connected to the exact independent variable of interest, namely therapist-led versus self-led VR with cognitive therapy. In addition, a few references are used somewhat loosely or are not the strongest possible support for key claims, and there are some factual imprecisions in how prior studies are characterized. Overall, though, the introduction clearly meets the criteria for a coherent, relevant, and mostly convincing rationale.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is well aligned with the course goal of evaluating scientific reasoning rather than publication-level polish. A strength is that it explicitly distinguishes between mere study summary and genuine synthesis, which is crucial for second-year students. One possible refinement would be to operationalize more clearly how much weakness in one component can be compensated by strength in another. For example, the rubric mentions all major components from the writing guide, but it is not always obvious how to weigh a strong theoretical framework against weaker societal relevance or vice versa. Adding a few anchor examples for what counts as 'somewhat synthesized' versus 'mostly synthesized' could improve inter-rater consistency.
methods_feedback:
The methods section describes a coherent study design that is clearly related to the stated research question and hypothesis. The sample, assignment to conditions, screening procedure, treatment conditions, number of sessions, and measurement moments are all reported. Participants, materials, and procedure are generally understandable, and the intended design can be followed without major confusion. For this course level, that supports an Adequate to low-Good evaluation.

A strength is that the section contains most of the key structural elements requested in the writing guide: inclusion and exclusion criteria, allocation to conditions, basic demographics, a main outcome measure with scoring information, and a chronological procedure. The treatment subsection also gives a reasonably clear picture of how therapist-led and self-led interventions differ.

The main weaknesses are missing or imprecise methodological details. The LSAS-SR is described as a screening and outcome measure, but the wording about what it screens for is inaccurate, and the use of screening scores as pre-treatment scores raises design concerns that are not addressed. The materials section is relatively sparse for the intervention itself; critical details about how the cognitive therapy component was standardized, how the AI assistant functioned, and how equivalence between conditions was ensured are not described in enough depth. There is also some information placed in less-than-ideal locations, with treatment details separated from Materials and Procedure in a way that slightly blurs structure. Finally, some practical choices are not well justified, such as recruitment through a podcast, lack of compensation, and all therapist-led sessions taking place in the lab while self-led sessions occur at home, which introduces more differences than just therapist guidance. These issues lower the score somewhat, but the design remains coherent and mostly complete.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric gives a useful balance between conceptual coherence and completeness. Its emphasis on whether the design matches the RQ and hypothesis is especially appropriate for this course. A possible improvement would be to specify more explicitly which missing details count as 'important' versus 'minor,' since that distinction likely determines movement between Developing and Adequate. It may also help to clarify how to judge design confounds that do not make the study incomprehensible but do weaken internal validity, because this is a common issue in student work.
results_feedback:
The results section reports the main analysis in a way that is mostly coherent and relevant to the stated design. The mixed ANOVA is appropriate for the 2 x 3 design, the key main effects and interaction are reported, assumptions are addressed, and post-hoc comparisons are used to interpret the interaction. This matches the basic expectations of the rubric.

However, the section is clearly weaker than the sample standard in terms of completeness and presentation. Most importantly, Table 1 and Table 2 are referenced but not actually presented in proper table form within the results section; instead, their contents appear appended after the references. Figure 1 is also described but not actually shown. Because the rubric and calibration explicitly expect descriptive tables and a plot, this missing presentation limits the score. The reporting is understandable, but not fully complete in the expected format.

There are also some smaller issues with statistical reporting. The results refer to LSAS-SR average scores, while the scale has been described earlier in total-score terms, which creates some inconsistency. Assumption checking is somewhat selective, and the rationale for ignoring the homogeneity violation is brief. Still, the main inferential conclusions are interpretable and tied to the hypothesis, so this section fits the Adequate band rather than Developing.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is appropriately anchored to the provided sample, which helps standardize expectations. Its focus on completeness, coherence, and relevance is useful. A potential limitation is that it treats the presence of expected elements somewhat globally; more explicit separation between statistical appropriateness and reporting/presentation quality could improve transparency. For instance, missing tables or figures and flawed interpretation of an otherwise correct analysis are both currently folded into the same descriptor. Distinguishing those subdimensions could make grading more consistent.
discussion_feedback:
The discussion provides a correct and mostly coherent interpretation of the findings. It opens by revisiting the aim and hypothesis and clearly states which parts were supported and which were only partially supported. The student then connects the findings back to previous literature and to the theoretical accounts introduced earlier, especially conditioning and cognitive perspectives. This shows real engagement with the introduction rather than treating the discussion as an isolated section.

A clear strength is the handling of the unexpected long-term result for the self-led condition. The student does not ignore it, but attempts to explain it by comparing the broader exposure content in the present study with the public-speaking focus in Lindner et al. This is exactly the sort of interpretive move expected at this level. The discussion also includes study-specific limitations and future directions, especially concerning the absence of a waiting-list control and uncertainty about engagement in the self-led condition.

What keeps the score from the Good range is that some interpretive steps are still too speculative or insufficiently grounded. For example, the argument that self-led improvements may reflect spontaneous symptom reduction or regression to the mean is plausible, but it sits somewhat awkwardly alongside the earlier strong claims about significant treatment effects and is not fully developed. Similarly, some implications extend beyond what the design can support, especially when discussing accessibility and adoption. The discussion links theory and literature back to the findings reasonably well, but not always with the strongest precision. Overall, it is a solid, mostly complete discussion with relevant critical reflection, but not consistently convincing enough for a higher score.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric captures the most important learning goals very well: drawing a justified conclusion, linking back to the introduction, comparing with prior research, and giving study-specific limitations and future directions. A helpful refinement could be to make explicit how much weight should be given to handling unexpected findings, since this is often a defining quality marker in discussions. It may also be useful to clarify what counts as a 'study-specific' limitation versus a generic one with a study-specific justification, as that boundary can be fuzzy in practice.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally readable and uses an appropriate scientific tone. Most sections are clearly structured, terminology is mostly consistent, and the reader can follow the main argument without major difficulty. Paragraphing is functional, and the overall organization follows the expected structure of an empirical paper.

At the same time, there are enough language, formatting, and APA-related issues to keep this in the Adequate range rather than Good. There are multiple citation and reference inconsistencies, including mismatches in publication years, formatting irregularities, duplicate or potentially confused references, and non-APA reference formats for some entries. There are also minor wording issues and awkward phrasings throughout. In addition, the presentation of tables and figure material is not cleanly integrated into the paper, which affects overall style and layout.

These issues do not seriously impede understanding, so they should not heavily lower the content grades. But for the Language & Style component itself, they are substantial enough to prevent a higher mark.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is strong in that it prevents language issues from overshadowing scientific reasoning in the other sections. Its descriptors are concrete enough to be practical, especially the attention to structure, ambiguity, and terminology consistency. One possible refinement is that counting errors alone may not fully reflect communicative quality; a paper with several minor APA mistakes can still read more clearly than one with fewer but more disruptive problems. It might therefore help to distinguish mechanical correctness from reader-level clarity even more explicitly.

intro_feedback: The introduction contains a clear and relevant research question and ends with a specific hypothesis that follows logically from the preceding argument. Societal relevance is present early and is aligned with the population and design. The paper also includes the required core studies and an additional study, and prior research is generally used to build toward the comparison between therapist-led and self-led VR. The theoretical background is stronger than average for this level: CBT, exposure/extinction, and cognitive mechanisms are explained and linked to why therapist involvement may matter. The main reason this does not reach the excellent range is that some links in the reasoning are still somewhat stretched or underdeveloped. For example, the jump from evidence on therapist-led VR versus in vivo to a hypothesis about therapist-led versus self-led VR is reasonable but not fully substantiated with direct evidence, and some claims about home-based accessibility and long-term relapse prevention are asserted more strongly than they are empirically supported. Overall, however, the line of reasoning is coherent, relevant, and convincingly argued for this course level.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is strong in emphasizing line of reasoning, synthesis, and the role of prior research, which matches the course focus well. A useful refinement would be to distinguish more explicitly between weak synthesis and weak theoretical substantiation, because students may do one better than the other. The rubric could also clarify how to judge introductions that include all required components but rely on partially indirect or speculative links between studies and hypotheses. At present, the bands sometimes combine too many criteria with AND/OR, which can make borderline decisions less transparent.
methods_feedback: The method section describes a coherent design that matches the stated research question and hypothesis: a randomized comparison between therapist-led and self-led VR with repeated measurements over time. Participants, inclusion/exclusion criteria, assignment to conditions, core materials, and the broad treatment structure are all present. The section is understandable and mostly complete, but it lacks several important details expected in the writing guide. The LSAS-SR is used both for screening and outcome measurement, but the description incorrectly refers to generalized anxiety disorder rather than social anxiety disorder, which is a substantive weakness. The treatment description is informative, yet key standardization details remain vague, especially because scenarios were individualized in order and intensity, making it less clear how comparability between conditions was ensured. There is also some structural awkwardness, with treatment details separated from materials and procedure in a way that makes replication somewhat harder. In addition, using screening LSAS-SR scores as pre-treatment scores raises a design concern that is not justified. Still, the design remains coherent and largely aligned with the RQ, so this fits the adequate range.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately prioritizes coherence with the RQ and completeness according to the writing guide. It would be even more usable if it specified which missing details count as major versus minor omissions, since not all absent details should affect the grade equally. In particular, it could more explicitly separate replication-relevant omissions from formatting or subsection-placement issues. That would help calibrate grades more consistently across papers that are understandable but not perfectly structured.
results_feedback: The results section reports the main analysis appropriately for the stated design: a mixed ANOVA with time, condition, and their interaction, followed by post-hoc comparisons. The reporting is coherent and the interpretation of the significant interaction is clear. Assumptions are discussed at an acceptable student level, and the narrative of the results generally matches the hypothesis. However, the section is notably incomplete relative to the sample expectations. The text refers to Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 1, but these are not properly integrated in standard report format, and the results do not include the full level of descriptive reporting suggested by the sample. The demographic and outcome information is present only in a compressed form at the end, rather than as clearly formatted tables within the section. There is also no fuller reporting of degrees of freedom or exact structure for all post-hoc comparisons beyond the main narrative. Because the key elements are present but somewhat underdeveloped and not fully in line with the sample template, this falls in the adequate range.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is helpfully anchored to the sample section and gives concrete expectations about tables, tests, post-hoc analyses, and a figure. That makes grading more reliable. A possible improvement would be to clarify how much weight should be given to missing formatting elements versus the correctness of the actual statistical reasoning. Right now, a paper with correct interpretation but incomplete visual/tabular reporting may be difficult to distinguish from one with more serious analytic weaknesses. A finer distinction within the adequate band could improve consistency.
discussion_feedback: The discussion gives a clear answer to the research question and distinguishes well between supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis. It meaningfully connects the findings back to prior research and to the theoretical ideas introduced earlier, especially around extinction, cognitive components, and therapist personalization. The student also engages with an unexpected pattern: self-led effects were maintained over time despite the expectation that they would diminish. This is interpreted rather than ignored, which is a strength. The critical reflection is study-specific and includes more than generic limitations, such as the lack of a waiting-list control and inability to assess engagement in the self-led condition. Future directions are concrete and logically derived from those limitations. The main weakness is that some claims in the discussion are stronger than the results justify, particularly the suggestion that self-led improvement may reflect spontaneous reduction or regression to the mean, which is plausible but speculative without a control group. Some comparisons to prior studies are also a bit selective. Still, overall the discussion is coherent, relevant, and meaningfully argued, placing it in the good range.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric aligns well with the course goals by emphasizing interpretation, linkage to the introduction, and study-specific critical reflection. It is especially useful that generic limitations are explicitly discouraged. One improvement would be to operationalize what counts as a meaningful link back to theory, because this can vary a lot between markers. The rubric could also clarify how to treat discussions that are strong on limitations and implications but somewhat speculative in interpreting unexpected findings.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear, readable, and well organized. Paragraphs usually have a single focus and the argument is easy to follow. Terminology is mostly consistent, and the scientific tone is appropriate for the assignment. The main issues are with APA and precision rather than readability. There are several reference inaccuracies and inconsistencies, including year mismatches, formatting issues, non-APA reference entries, duplicated Wang et al. references, and some imprecise source descriptions. There are also a few awkward or overly strong phrasings and some minor wording problems. These issues do not seriously impede comprehension, but they are too frequent for a good or excellent language/style score. Overall, the writing is satisfactory and clear, with moderate APA and style weaknesses.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is practical because it keeps language from overpowering content grading, which suits this course well. The inclusion of terminology consistency is particularly helpful. However, the use of hard numerical cutoffs for grammar and APA errors may give a false sense of precision and may be difficult to apply consistently across markers. It may be better to combine counts with severity and impact on readability. Also, clearer distinction between APA layout errors and citation/reference accuracy would improve precision.

intro_feedback: The introduction presents a clear and relevant research question and builds toward it with a generally coherent argumentative line. Societal relevance is established early and is aligned with the proposed design, and the paper includes the three required core studies plus additional literature. The theoretical section is stronger than a simple literature summary: it discusses cognitive and behavioral perspectives, extinction, and why therapist guidance might matter. Prior research is mostly used as building blocks rather than only being reviewed, and the final hypothesis follows logically from the preceding argument. The main weakness is that some links are still somewhat overstated or not fully substantiated. For example, claims about at-home VR increasing treatment adoption and about the superiority of therapist-led treatment are plausible, but the reasoning is not always equally well supported by prior empirical work. In addition, some parts of the previous-research section still read study-by-study rather than fully synthesized. Overall, this fits the good band: sound, coherent, and clearly leading to the RQ and hypothesis, with a few weaker links.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is strong in emphasizing argumentative coherence, relevance of the RQ, and synthesis of prior research rather than summary. A possible improvement would be to distinguish more explicitly between weaknesses in theoretical framing versus weaknesses in empirical synthesis, because both currently sit under the same broad criterion. The rubric could also clarify how heavily missing one required core article should weigh relative to having all articles but using them poorly.
methods_feedback: The method section describes a coherent design that is related to the stated research question and hypothesis. Participants, screening, allocation to condition, broad treatment structure, and measurement moments are all included, and the distinction between therapist-led and self-led VR is described clearly enough to understand the intended manipulation. However, the section lacks some important detail expected from the writing guide. The participant description misses fuller sample information and does not explain recruitment feasibility or ethical/practical implications of the sampling strategy. The materials section is incomplete: the LSAS-SR is described reasonably well, but the intervention itself is only partly operationalized, and the cognitive therapy component is not described in enough detail to allow clear replication. Important measurement details are also unclear, such as whether the LSAS-SR served both as screening and baseline outcome without contamination concerns. There is also some structural misplacement: the intervention description appears under a separate Treatment heading after Procedure, rather than being more cleanly integrated into Materials/Procedure according to the guide. These are meaningful but not fatal issues, so the section is adequate rather than good.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately focuses on coherence with the RQ and completeness of participants, materials, and procedure. It may benefit from more explicit anchors for what counts as an 'important detail' at this course level, for example randomization, measurement moments, operationalization of the manipulation, and questionnaire scoring. That would make distinctions between developing and adequate more transparent and consistent across graders.
results_feedback: The results section is coherent and the chosen analysis matches the stated design: a mixed ANOVA for condition by time is appropriate, assumptions are briefly addressed, and the main effects, interaction, and Holm-corrected post hoc comparisons are reported in an understandable way. However, compared with the sample and rubric expectations, the section is incomplete in presentation. The text refers to Table 1, Table 2, and Figure 1, but the actual paper does not present them in standard integrated format; instead, the numerical content appears detached at the end, which weakens clarity and reporting quality. The sample expectations also point toward full descriptive tables and a plot clearly embedded in the section, and here those elements are only partially realized. In addition, the reporting is somewhat thin: there are no effect sizes, the assumption checks are selective, and the description of the means raises interpretive concerns because symptom decreases are statistically significant but numerically modest in one condition. Still, the core analysis is relevant and mostly correct. This places the section in the developing range rather than adequate.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is usefully concrete because it ties grading to the sample section and expected elements. It could be improved by clarifying how to weigh missing presentation elements versus correct statistical reasoning. For instance, a paper may have the right analysis but poorly integrated tables/figures; clearer guidance on whether that is primarily a Results issue or partly a Language/Style issue would support more consistent grading.
discussion_feedback: The discussion answers the research question clearly, distinguishes between supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis, and meaningfully compares the findings with earlier studies. It also links the findings back to the theoretical framework from the introduction, especially conditioning, cognition, safety behaviors, and relapse/generalization. The paper does more than restate results: it interprets why therapist-led treatment may have outperformed self-led treatment and why the unexpected long-term maintenance in the self-led group may have occurred. The limitations are study-specific rather than generic, and the future research suggestions follow from those limitations. The main weakness is that some interpretations go somewhat beyond the data. For example, the argument that the self-led effect may reflect spontaneous improvement or regression to the mean is plausible, but it is speculative and only partly reconciled with the significant within-group reductions. Similarly, some broader implications are a little strong given the absence of a waiting-list condition and the modest effects in the self-led group. Overall, the reasoning is correct and mostly coherent, with relevant critical reflection and a solid link back to introduction and theory, placing it in the adequate-to-good range.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric captures the main priorities of this assignment well: correct conclusion, critical reflection, and linkage back to introduction and theory. A useful refinement would be to define more concretely what qualifies as a study-specific limitation versus a generic one, and what counts as a meaningful comparison to previous research. That would help distinguish adequate from good more reliably.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally clear and readable, with mostly appropriate scientific language and consistent terminology. Paragraph structure is usually logical, and the reader can follow the argument across sections. There are, however, several language and APA issues that prevent a higher score. Some sentences are overly long or slightly awkward, and there are a number of formatting inconsistencies in references, punctuation, capitalization, and citation style. There are also several factual/reference inconsistencies visible in the reference list and citations (e.g., year mismatches, unusual formatting, duplicate or potentially incorrect entries), and the presentation of tables is not polished. These issues do not usually impede understanding, but they are too frequent for the good band. Overall, the writing is satisfactory and functional, which fits the adequate band.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and practical, especially in covering structure, ambiguity, redundancy, APA, and terminology consistency. The numerical thresholds for grammar and APA errors are helpful but may encourage counting over judging impact. It may be better to supplement those thresholds with a stronger emphasis on how much the issues affect readability and professionalism, especially for papers with many minor but low-impact errors.

intro_feedback:
The Introduction shows a clear topic, a relevant research question, and an identifiable hypothesis. It also makes a real attempt to build a theoretical line from SAD mechanisms to exposure, then to VR exposure, and finally to the comparison between individual and group VR with a waitlist baseline. That gives the section a coherent overall direction, which places it above merely developing work. The societal relevance is present and linked to treatment accessibility. The theoretical framework is also more than descriptive: the paper uses ideas such as maladaptive cognitions, avoidance, inhibitory learning, expectancy violation, social modeling, and normalization to justify the expected superiority of group VR.

At the same time, the reasoning is only somewhat convincing rather than strongly convincing. Several references are weakly chosen for this assignment context or used in a way that does not fully support the claim being made, including website-like or general-information sources where stronger empirical sources would have been preferable. Some of the prior-research section is also historically and logically uneven: the required core studies are discussed, but the storyline between them is not always accurate or sharply synthesized, and the paper sometimes treats waitlist and active control logic in a slightly mechanical way rather than fully integrating why each study matters for the present design. There is also some overstatement in concluding that group VR should be superior, because the evidence base presented supports that possibility but not overwhelmingly. Overall, the Introduction is coherent and relevant, but not consistently persuasive or precise enough for a higher score.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric appropriately prioritizes the line of reasoning toward the research question, relevance, and hypothesis, which matches the course emphasis on argumentation. A useful refinement would be to distinguish more explicitly between 'coherent' and 'convincingly argued' by giving concrete indicators such as quality of literature synthesis, alignment between theory and hypothesis, and appropriateness of source selection. The current rubric mentions irresponsible references only at the insufficient level, but source quality matters across all levels and could be specified more continuously.
methods_feedback:
The Methods section presents the major expected components: participants, materials, and procedure. The design is understandable and related to the stated research question and hypotheses. Random allocation is described, the three conditions are clear, the main dependent measure is identified, and the broad procedure from pre-test to post-test is readable. This makes the method section passable in structure.

However, it falls below adequate because several important details are incomplete, unclear, or conceptually inconsistent. In the Participants section, the age reporting is incomplete ('Sixty participants ( 36, SD = 8.9...)' leaves out the mean label), and the diagnostic criterion 'DSM-5, no older than three years old' is confusing. The pharmacological exclusion criterion is also unclearly phrased ('not older than a year'). More importantly, the treatment conditions are described as exposure conditions, but they also include cognitive restructuring, which creates a mismatch with the Introduction's framing of exposure-only VR versus earlier CBT-based studies. That conceptual inconsistency matters because it affects whether the design really tests the stated hypothesis. The materials description of LSAS-SR is acceptable but not fully complete at the expected level: it lacks a proper developer citation in the standard way and gives only minimal psychometric information. Procedure is understandable, but some details needed for reproducibility are missing, such as how diagnosis was established, how group sessions were organized across weeks, and whether the same therapist treated all conditions. So the section is coherent enough to follow, but not complete and correct enough for an adequate score.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric captures the core issue well: coherence with the research question and completeness/correctness of participants, materials, and procedure. It could be improved by making explicit which omissions are relatively minor versus which are conceptually serious. For example, missing a reward detail is not equivalent to an unclear manipulation or a design-hypothesis mismatch. Adding anchor examples for expected detail at this course level would make scoring more consistent across assessors.
results_feedback:
The Results section follows the general expected structure reasonably well: it begins with sample use and outlier checks, reports assumptions, presents a mixed ANOVA aligned with the design, and interprets the interaction using post-hoc comparisons. The main findings are reported clearly enough for this level: both active treatments improved, the waitlist did not, and the two VR conditions did not differ significantly. This is coherent and relevant to the stated hypotheses.

The section does lose points because the reporting is incomplete and somewhat messy compared with the sample standard. The table presentation is severely disorganized in the submitted text, with duplicated labels and formatting problems that make the descriptive information harder to read than it should be. There is also no clean demographics table in the expected format, and the descriptive table structure is much less polished than the course sample. In addition, the assumption-check paragraph is slightly inconsistent with the full table, because one post-treatment Shapiro-Wilk value in the waitlist condition appears significant in the table, while the prose states normality was not violated based on the cited tests. The results are still mostly interpretable and the core inferential analysis matches the design, so this is above developing, but the incompleteness and inconsistency keep it from good.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is sensible in focusing on correctness, completeness, coherence, and relevance to the stated design. Its usefulness would increase if it incorporated some concrete course-specific anchors from the sample results, such as expectation of descriptive tables, assumption checks, clear reporting of the main analysis, and follow-up tests for interactions. That would help distinguish between adequate and good more transparently, especially for student work that is statistically correct but poorly organized.
discussion_feedback:
The Discussion is one of the stronger parts of the paper. It clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between the supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis. The interpretation is mostly at the construct level rather than just repeating statistics. The paper connects the supported effect of VR exposure to inhibitory learning and expectancy violation, and it engages directly with the unexpected null difference between group and individual VR. It also compares the findings to earlier work, especially Kampmann et al. and Anderson et al., and tries to explain why expected group advantages may not have emerged in this particular VR format.

The critical reflection is relevant and more specific than generic template limitations. The paper discusses limited interpersonal engagement in the group condition, broad age range and possible differences in technological familiarity, and absence of follow-up assessments. It also provides concrete future research directions tied to those limitations. The final paragraph returns to societal relevance and practical implications in a way that broadly follows from the findings.

The section is not higher because some explanations remain speculative and are not always tightly grounded in what was actually measured in the study. For example, claims about the quality of interpersonal engagement, normalization, or age-related VR fluency are plausible but were not directly assessed, so they need more careful framing. The discussion also does not fully address a key design issue: the method appears to include cognitive restructuring, which complicates claims about testing VR exposure effects alone. Even so, the reasoning toward the main conclusion is coherent and relevant, making this a good discussion for this course level.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric rightly centers on the reasoning toward the main conclusion and the relevance of the critical reflection. A helpful refinement would be to separate interpretation, integration with prior literature/theory, and critical evaluation into more visible subcriteria. At present, these are bundled together, which can make it hard to judge why one discussion is 'adequate' and another 'good.' More explicit attention to whether limitations are study-specific and whether implications actually follow from results would also improve reliability.
lang_style_feedback:
The paper is generally understandable and the section structure is clear, so the language does not prevent comprehension. Most paragraphs have an identifiable main point, and the writer uses scientific-signaling phrases often enough to guide the reader. That said, the writing quality is uneven and remains below adequate overall because there are frequent grammar, punctuation, wording, and APA-style issues.

Examples include awkward or incorrect phrasing, sentence-level redundancy, article and tense problems, inconsistent capitalization, citation formatting issues, and several unclear formulations. There are also noticeable APA/reference problems, such as inconsistent journal/source formatting, unusual source choices, citation punctuation errors, and reference-list inaccuracies. The tables are especially poorly formatted in the submitted version, which strongly affects presentation quality. Because the writing is mostly understandable but clearly contains some recurring errors and ambiguity, the language and style fit best with a developing-level score.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is detailed and useful, especially in noting structure, grammar, APA, ambiguity, and redundancy. One challenge is that several descriptors overlap strongly across levels, which may reduce inter-rater consistency. It may help to distinguish more clearly between readability problems that merely reduce polish and those that impair scientific meaning. Since APA is only 10% in the calibration summary, the rubric could also clarify that APA problems should matter mainly when they are systematic or interfere with traceability, rather than minor formatting imperfections.

intro_feedback: The Introduction presents a clear topic, establishes societal relevance, and ends with a reasonably clear aim and hypothesis. The student also attempts a theoretical framework around maladaptive cognitions, safety behaviors, inhibitory learning, expectancy violation, and possible group processes, which fits the course aim of building a line of reasoning rather than only summarizing studies. The research question is relevant and understandable. However, the line of reasoning is only moderately coherent. Several claims are asserted too strongly or with limited support, and the literature review does not sufficiently align with the required core set: Bouchard et al. (2017), Kampmann et al. (2016), and Anderson et al. (2013) are included, but the fourth article is used in a way that does not always integrate smoothly with the rest of the narrative. There are also substantive issues in how prior studies are characterized, with some oversimplification and some imprecise transitions from one study to the next. The argument that group VR should outperform individual VR is plausible, but not consistently developed from theory and prior evidence. Overall, the Introduction is coherent enough to be adequate, but not yet convincingly argued enough for a good score.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric appropriately emphasizes the line of reasoning toward the RQ, scientific relevance, and hypothesis. A useful refinement would be to make literature synthesis more explicit, because students can meet the current wording while still writing a study-by-study summary with only loose integration. It may also help to specify alignment with the required prior research set and theoretical framework, since coherence in this assignment depends strongly on linking theory, previous studies, and design choices.
methods_feedback: The Method section describes the basic design clearly enough: participants, three conditions, one main dependent variable, and a pre-post procedure. The design is related to the stated research question and hypotheses. The participant section includes sample size, mean age, age range, gender proportions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, allocation, and compensation, which matches several expected elements. However, there are important weaknesses that prevent a higher score. Some criteria are confusing or inconsistent (e.g., diagnosis timing and pharmacological therapy timing are phrased unclearly). The methods also contain a mismatch between the theoretical framing of exposure-only VR and the actual intervention description, which includes cognitive restructuring, making the design less cleanly aligned with the introduction. The materials section provides only limited information about how the protocol was standardized across group and individual formats, and the questionnaire description is incomplete at student level because reliability is mentioned vaguely and no source is given for that statement in the section itself. Procedure is mostly chronological, but still includes intervention detail that blurs the materials/procedure distinction. Overall, the method is mostly understandable and nearly complete, but there are enough conceptual and reporting issues to keep it in the developing range.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric captures coherence and completeness well, but it could more explicitly distinguish between minor reporting omissions and conceptual design mismatches. At present, a section can seem 'complete' while still being weakly aligned with the stated hypothesis or while mixing materials and procedure. Adding criteria about internal consistency between Introduction and Methods, and about sufficient detail for replication at student level, would make the rubric more precise.
results_feedback: The Results section follows the expected overall structure reasonably well: outliers are mentioned, assumptions are addressed, the mixed ANOVA is reported, and post-hoc tests are interpreted in relation to the design. The main findings are clearly communicated, and the interpretation of the interaction is appropriate. This is broadly in line with the sample structure and therefore sits around adequate to good for this course level. However, there are notable problems. The presentation of tables is very messy and repetitive, making parts of the section difficult to read. The text refers to tables inconsistently, and a demographics table in the expected clean format is not properly presented. There is also an inconsistency in the normality reporting: the prose says normality was not violated, but one post-treatment p-value in the table appears significant for one condition. In addition, the section reports some analysis output that suggests age may have been included, but this is not clearly explained in the main text. These issues reduce coherence and completeness, but the core analysis and substantive reporting remain mostly correct and relevant.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is broadly usable, especially with the sample results as calibration. It would benefit from clearer mention of expected structural elements for this course, such as a clean demographics table, descriptive statistics per condition/time, assumption checks at an appropriate level, and direct reporting of the main test tied to the design. The distinction between Adequate and Good could also be sharpened by specifying how much clarity, completeness, and consistency in tables/figures are expected.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion opens appropriately with the aim, hypotheses, and main findings at the construct level. It clearly distinguishes the supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis, compares the findings to theory, and tries to explain the unexpected null difference between the two active conditions. The student also links the results back to prior literature, especially Kampmann et al. (2016) and Anderson et al. (2013), and includes multiple limitations and future directions. This is a solid discussion for this course level. Still, the reasoning is not fully convincing throughout. Some explanations are speculative and not always tightly grounded in the present design or data. The discussion of theory is somewhat repetitive, especially around expectancy violation, and some cited sources are used loosely. One limitation is discussed in a somewhat self-protective way rather than critically evaluating the strength of the study, and some broader implications are a little stronger than the data justify. Even so, the section is mostly coherent, relevant, and appropriately reflective, which supports an adequate-to-good score.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric rightly focuses on the reasoning toward the main conclusion and the relevance of critical reflection. A possible improvement would be to state more explicitly that good discussions should interpret both expected and unexpected findings, connect results back to the theory introduced earlier, and provide study-specific limitations and future directions. This would help distinguish a discussion that merely restates results from one that genuinely reasons from them.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and the intended scientific meaning is usually clear, but the language and style contain enough issues to lower the score. There are repeated grammar, punctuation, capitalization, spacing, and phrasing problems. Sentence structure is sometimes awkward or imprecise, and several statements are redundant or overly long. APA style is inconsistent in both in-text citations and the reference list, with formatting errors, spelling errors in source names, inconsistent capitalization, and some questionable or non-ideal source choices. The Results tables are especially poorly formatted, which harms readability. At the paragraph level, structure is usually visible, but not always tight: some paragraphs contain more than one main point and transitions can be abrupt. Because the writing does not impede overall understanding but is clearly below a polished standard, this fits the developing range.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is helpful in covering clarity, structure, grammar, APA, vagueness, and redundancy. However, it could be improved by separating language quality from APA/layout more clearly, since a paper can be readable but weak in formatting, or vice versa. It may also help to include clearer indicators of paragraph coherence and signposting, because these are especially important in argumentative student papers and not fully captured by sentence-level correctness alone.

intro_feedback: The Introduction presents a clear topic, a relevant broad problem, and a logically intended comparison between group VR, individual VR, and waitlist. The research question and hypothesis are ultimately understandable, and the paper does attempt to build a theoretical line through maladaptive cognitions, avoidance, inhibitory learning, and possible group mechanisms. That said, the line of reasoning is only moderately coherent. Several sources are used in a way that is not always well aligned with the exact claims being made, and some references are not ideal for core substantiation of clinical claims. The theoretical framework is present, but it is somewhat diffuse: parts on exposure theory, group processes, and waitlist rationale are included, yet the transition from theory to the specific hypothesis is not consistently sharp. The prior research section also contains notable inaccuracies relative to the core literature expected in this course, especially in how some studies are characterized and linked. The overall storyline does reach a clear RQ, but the argument is only somewhat convincing rather than strongly compelling.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric captures the core course priority well by emphasizing the line of reasoning toward the RQ, scientific relevance, and hypothesis. A useful refinement would be to separate 'quality of literature synthesis' from 'clarity/relevance of the RQ,' because a paper can have a clear RQ but a weak argumentative buildup. It may also help to specify how inaccuracies in describing core studies should weigh relative to a generally coherent storyline.
methods_feedback: The Methods section describes a coherent three-condition design that matches the stated research question and hypotheses. Participants, materials, and procedure are all present, and the general setup is understandable. However, the section remains only partly complete and not fully precise. The participant description contains confusing inclusion/exclusion phrasing, especially around diagnosis age and medication criteria. Some method details that matter for replication are vague or inconsistent, such as how diagnosis was established, how randomization was implemented in practice, and whether the treatment is pure exposure or includes broader CBT components. The Materials section mixes procedural information with instrument description, and the measure description is somewhat limited for course expectations. Overall, the design is related to the RQ, but the description is only somewhat comprehensive and contains enough ambiguity to place it below adequate.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric appropriately prioritizes coherence between design and RQ, plus completeness of participants, materials, and procedure. To improve consistency between graders, the rubric could specify a few anchor elements that are expected for adequacy at this course level, such as allocation to conditions, inclusion/exclusion criteria, operationalization of the IV and DV, and enough procedural detail for reasonable replication. This would help distinguish 'nearly complete' from 'complete and correct.'
results_feedback: The Results section uses an appropriate overall analysis for the stated design: a 3 x 2 mixed ANOVA, followed by post-hoc comparisons. The main findings are clearly reported and are relevant to the hypotheses. Assumptions are addressed at a reasonable student level, and the interpretation of the interaction is understandable. The section benefits from providing test statistics and post-hoc results. However, there are important weaknesses in completeness and presentation. The tables are poorly integrated and formatted, the numbering is inconsistent, and the sample description table expected by the course is not cleanly presented. The text also contains some inconsistencies in referring to tables and assumptions, and the descriptive reporting is harder to follow than the sample structure provided in the course materials. Still, the core analysis and reporting are mostly correct and relevant, which supports an adequate-to-good range; given the formatting and coherence problems, the section fits best at adequate-plus.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is strong in focusing on correctness, completeness, coherence, and relevance to the design. It could be improved by explicitly including expected structural elements from the course sample, such as demographics/descriptive tables, assumption checks, reporting of main effects and interaction, and post-hoc follow-up where needed. This would make the jump from 'adequate' to 'good' easier to calibrate across markers.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion opens with a clear restatement of the aim and gives a direct answer to the research question. It correctly distinguishes between the supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis and makes a genuine attempt to interpret the null difference between the two active conditions. The student also connects findings back to inhibitory learning theory and prior literature, and includes multiple limitations plus future research directions. These are strengths. However, the discussion is not fully coherent or consistently well supported. Some explanations are plausible but remain speculative, and the integration with prior research is selective and sometimes overstates what earlier studies imply. Theoretical interpretation is present, but not always carefully bounded by what was actually tested. Some limitations are relevant, but parts of the argument defending the main conclusion are repetitive. The broader implications are present and generally appropriate, yet somewhat stronger than warranted given the design and results. Overall, this is a correct and relevant discussion, but only somewhat convincing rather than fully strong.
discussion_rubric_feedback: The Discussion rubric correctly emphasizes both the reasoning toward the main conclusion and the quality of critical reflection. A helpful refinement would be to make explicit that strong discussions should not merely restate results, but also integrate findings with prior research and theory, engage with unexpected findings, and provide study-specific limitations plus concrete future directions. These expectations are present in the writing guide but could be more visible in the rubric itself.
lang_style_feedback: The paper is generally understandable and uses mostly appropriate scientific language, but clarity is reduced by many sentence-level issues. There are frequent grammar, punctuation, spacing, capitalization, and wording problems. Some sentences are awkward or imprecise, and paragraph structure is uneven, with occasional redundancy and repetition. APA style is inconsistent in both references and in-text citations, and the reference list contains multiple formatting errors and some questionable source choices for scientific support. The tables are also poorly formatted and disrupt readability. Because the writing usually remains interpretable but is not consistently polished or well structured, this fits the developing range rather than adequate.
lang_style_rubric_feedback: The Language & Style rubric is useful because it covers readability, structure, grammar, APA, vagueness, and redundancy. To improve reliability, it may help to distinguish more clearly between language problems that merely reduce polish and those that materially obstruct scientific understanding. It could also note that formatting of tables/figures and reference quality are part of presentation quality at this level, while still keeping content separate from style.

intro_feedback: The Introduction contains a clear topic, a visible research question, and an overall argumentative line toward comparing group VR, individual VR, and a waitlist condition. Societal relevance is present early on, key constructs such as SAD, exposure, expectancy violation, and group processes are introduced, and the final paragraph states the aim and hypothesis clearly enough. This places the section above Developing. However, the argumentation is only mostly coherent rather than solidly convincing. Prior research is sometimes used as building blocks, but several transitions are weak or overstated, and some claims are not well supported by the cited evidence. The required core studies are not all integrated as expected: Kampmann, Anderson, and Bouchard are discussed, but the fourth article is not used as strongly as a study specifically sharpening the chosen design, and the line from prior findings to the hypothesis relies on several leaps. There are also source-quality issues in crucial places, including older or less appropriate references for central claims and some inaccurate or imprecise framing of treatment and DSM material. Overall, the Introduction fits the Adequate band: sound and mostly coherent, but not consistently convincing.
intro_rubric_feedback: The Introduction rubric is generally strong because it emphasizes argumentation quality, synthesis of prior research, and whether the RQ follows from the literature rather than rewarding mere inclusion of parts. A possible improvement would be to distinguish more explicitly between missing required content and weak causal logic, since these currently sit together within the same band descriptors. It may also help to clarify how much weight should be given to using all required core articles versus using them well, because students can technically include all studies while still producing weak synthesis.
methods_feedback: The Methods section presents the basic required subsections and the design is related to the stated research question and hypotheses. Participants, conditions, measure, and procedure are all described, and the reader can broadly understand what was done. This supports a Developing-to-Adequate level. The main limitation is that multiple important details are missing or unclear. The participant description is incomplete and somewhat confusing: the mean age is reported incorrectly or incompletely, inclusion and exclusion criteria are phrased unclearly, diagnostic verification is not well specified, and allocation details are minimal. In Materials, the treatment descriptions are understandable but mix procedural and material information, and the study is described as exposure-focused while the protocol also includes cognitive restructuring, which creates conceptual inconsistency with the Introduction and hypothesis. The questionnaire description is acceptable but limited, with little detail beyond item count, scale, and score range. Procedure is chronological and readable, but some details that matter for replication remain vague, such as who administered assessments, whether assessors were blinded, and how group sessions were standardized. Because the design is coherent and mostly understandable but lacks several important details, this section best fits Developing.
methods_rubric_feedback: The Methods rubric is useful in focusing on coherence with the RQ and the completeness of participants, materials, and procedure. It could be strengthened by naming a few high-priority details that matter most at this level, such as allocation/randomization, inclusion and exclusion criteria, operationalization of conditions, and measurement details. Right now, the distinction between Developing and Adequate can become subjective when a section is broadly understandable but missing several medium-importance details.
results_feedback: The Results section includes the expected core elements: descriptive information, assumption checks, the mixed ANOVA, interaction reporting, post-hoc comparisons, and a figure reference. The main analysis is appropriate for the stated design, and the interpretation of the significant interaction is generally correct. This places the section at least in the Adequate range. At the same time, the reporting is somewhat uneven and not fully coherent. The section refers to tables in a confusing way, there is no clean demographics table in the style expected by the sample, and the pasted tables are cluttered and difficult to read. Some assumption reporting is incomplete or selective: one post-treatment Shapiro-Wilk result appears to indicate non-normality, but the narrative says normality was not violated while only discussing pre-test values. There is also some inconsistency in table numbering and in how the reported tables map onto the text. Still, all major analytical elements are present, the statistical conclusions align with the reported values, and the section is relevant to the design. Therefore, the Results are mostly correct and complete, but not well enough executed for Good.
results_rubric_feedback: The Results rubric is appropriately anchored to the sample and gives concrete expectations for this course level. A helpful refinement would be to separate statistical correctness from presentation quality more explicitly. At present, a section with correct analyses but confusing tables and assumption reporting can be hard to place between Developing and Adequate. It may also help to specify whether all assumption checks must be reported completely or only those relevant to the chosen analysis.
discussion_feedback: The Discussion clearly restates the aim, answers the research question, and distinguishes between supported and unsupported parts of the hypothesis.
